transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

I'm a psychologist, and I've come in for an evaluation because my thoughts feel like they’re racing nonstop, jumping from idea to idea so fast that I can’t keep my head clear, even in sessions with my patients. It's deeply unsettling because I've always prided myself on careful self-monitoring, but right now I feel like I'm losing my cognitive grip.
Have you also been experiencing periods of persistent irritability, elevated mood, or an increased sense of energy along with these racing thoughts?

Yes, I've been swinging between feeling almost euphoric and invincible, and then getting irrationally snappy with my wife and colleagues over minor things. At the same time, I feel this relentless drive to keep producing, taking on extra clinic work and starting multiple projects at all hours because I just can't sit still.
Can you tell me how long you've been experiencing these episodes of racing thoughts, elevated mood, and increased energy, and whether they come and go or have been persistent over time?

This entire experience has been unfolding over the past few months, but it has shifted. The intense, high-energy surge with the racing thoughts and elevated mood was a temporary phase that has since passed, whereas this heavier, flatter, and guilt-ridden state has been persistently hanging over me for about the last four months.

Can you clarify if there were distinct periods where you experienced the high-energy, elevated mood state without the depressive symptoms, and if so, how long those periods typically lasted before shifting to the current state?

Yes, there was a very distinct, highly driven period that started right after I returned from a stimulating conference, and that intense, elevated state lasted for about a month without any depression. Once that surge faded, I transitioned directly into this heavy, flat state which has now been dominant for the last four months.

Can you estimate how many days or weeks the elevated mood and high-energy state lasted before you transitioned into the depressive state, and have you experienced any similar episodes of elevated mood in the past?

The elevated, high-energy phase lasted for about a month after I returned from my conference, right before I transitioned into this depressive state that has now been going on for about four months. I have never experienced an episode like this in the past, as I've always prided myself on maintaining a careful balance and self-monitoring.

Can you confirm if the month-long period of elevated mood and high energy was completely free of depressive symptoms, and did it meet a full two weeks of duration with at least three symptoms of mania or hypomania?

Actually, looking back, that high-energy month wasn't completely free of depressive symptoms; those flat feelings and dark thoughts have been looming for about four months, overlapping even as that surge came and went. That intense phase lasted well over two weeks—about a month—and definitely involved multiple symptoms like my racing thoughts, pressured speech, insomnia, and taking on far too many activities.

Did the month-long period of elevated mood and high energy significantly impact your daily life or relationships in a noticeable way, such as requiring hospitalization or causing problems at work or with your family?

Yes, it has severely disrupted both my career and my marriage. At the clinic, I was pulled from leading my new program and had to transfer several patients after concerns were raised about my clinical judgment. At home, my wife feels like she is living with a stranger who is constantly working, pacing, or arguing instead of being present with her.

Can you further clarify if there were any periods where you experienced depressive symptoms concurrently with the manic or hypomanic symptoms, or if these states occurred distinctly separate from one another?

The states actually overlapped significantly, as the low mood, loss of interest, and darker thoughts have been present for about four months, persisting even during that high-energy surge. Even while running on high energy, I felt a bone-deep fatigue underneath and intense guilt if I slowed down for a moment, though the humming voice I heard only occurred during those peak manic periods.
You mentioned hearing a humming voice during the peak manic periods, can you tell me more about this experience, such as what the voice said or how it made you feel?

In my closed office, I would hear what sounded like a woman humming a specific tune and occasionally saying my name, and it felt like an actual, physical sound in the room rather than just a thought. It was incredibly unsettling to experience as a psychologist, but in those highly wired moments, I felt convinced the voice was guiding me on what to do next with my patients. This only occurred when my mood was ramped up and my sleep had collapsed, disappearing completely once I crashed into this low state.

Can you confirm if the humming voice you heard during the manic periods was the only psychotic symptom you experienced, or were there any other hallucinations or delusions present during that time or at any other point?

No, the humming voice wasn't the only thing; I also felt convinced that I was receiving special insights and instructions from artwork and song lyrics to guide my treatment decisions. Both the voice and those symbolic insights occurred exclusively during those highly wired, sleep-deprived manic periods. Once I crashed into this lower, depressed state, those experiences completely disappeared.

Did you ever lose touch with reality or have difficulty distinguishing between the humming voice, special insights, and your own thoughts during the manic periods, or were you always aware that these experiences were unusual and not part of everyday reality?

During those manic periods, I completely lost touch with reality and genuinely believed those experiences were real, feeling convinced that the humming was an actual sound in the room and that the insights from art were truly guiding my clinical decisions. It was only after a trusted colleague confronted me about a risky decision and my mood began to shift that I had the distressing realization that I had lost touch with reality and could no longer trust my own judgment.

Can you describe if the depressive symptoms you've been experiencing for the last four months have included any psychotic symptoms, such as hallucinations or delusions, similar to those you experienced during the manic periods?

No, those psychotic symptoms have not occurred at all during the depressive periods. They only happen when my mood is highly ramped up and my sleep is completely disrupted. During these low, exhausted, and guilty stretches, the voice and the special insights disappear completely.
Did the presence of psychotic symptoms, such as the humming voice and special insights, only occur during the manic or hypomanic episodes, or were they also present during any periods of depression?

Yes, the humming voice and the special insights only occurred during the high-energy, wired periods when my mood was ramped up and my sleep fell apart. They faded away completely during the low, exhausted, and guilty stretches, and have not been present at all during my depression.

You've mentioned that the psychotic symptoms, like the humming voice and special insights, only occurred during the manic periods and not during the depressive episodes. Can you confirm if these psychotic symptoms were present for the majority of the time during those manic periods, or were they episodic and occurring only at the peak of your manic symptoms?

I'm not entirely sure about the exact proportion of time. I can't really confirm if it was the majority of the time or just the absolute peak, but those experiences definitely seemed tied to when my mind was racing the fastest and my sleep was at its worst.

Can you confirm if the psychotic symptoms, such as the humming voice and special insights, were directly related to the intensity of your manic symptoms, and did they disappear completely when you transitioned into the depressive state?

Yes, I can confirm that. The humming voice and those special insights only occurred when my mood was highly elevated and my sleep was at its worst. Once I transitioned into this low, drained, and guilty state, those experiences faded away completely.

Did the presence of psychotic symptoms during the manic periods influence your diagnosis, considering they are not present during the depressive episodes, and how do you think this distinction affects your overall condition?

As a psychologist, I recognize that this distinction is clinically crucial because it confirms the psychotic features are tied directly to my manic episodes rather than indicating a continuous, primary psychotic disorder. The humming voice and special insights only happened when I was highly wired and sleep-deprived, disappearing completely once I transitioned into this low, depressive state. Understanding that these symptoms are bound to the mania helps me make sense of a Bipolar I diagnosis and gives me some much-needed clarity during a very disorienting time.
